First read vs progressions

FTN charting records which read each pass went to. In scheme means the throw the play was built for: a designed throw (mostly screens) or the first read. Past the first read means he worked to his second read or the checkdown. FTN doesn't chart third and fourth reads separately; the checkdown is the last read. Charting starts in 2022, so the career window here is 2022–26 for both quarterbacks.

How each dropback ends

Share of his dropbacks by the read the ball went to, or by sack or scramble when no pass was thrown.

Supporting cast

Every receiver he targeted, compared with the same receiver's whole career on targets from other quarterbacks (2006 on). The cast baseline is what his targets would be worth if his receivers did what they did with other passers. A receiver with little history away from him counts as roughly average for his position. Lift is his result minus that baseline. Proven receivers are those with 100 or more targets from other quarterbacks; lift on them alone is the cleaner comparison. Rating is passer rating when targeted.

EPA per target: with him vs his cast's baseline

Solid line: what his targets produced. Dashed line: what the same receivers produced for other quarterbacks, weighted by how often he threw to each. The shaded gap between them is his lift.

Coaching and context

How much of each offense is the quarterback, and how much is the play-caller, the receivers, the schedule and the game situation? A model of every offensive play since 2006 credits each play to its quarterback, play-caller and opposing defense, while accounting for down, distance, field position, score and the receivers' record with other passers. Quarterbacks change play-callers and play-callers coach several quarterbacks, which is what lets the model separate them. Thin samples are pulled toward average. All games.

Where each offense's edge comes from

EPA per play above league average on the plays each quarterback was on the field, split into play-caller, quarterback, supporting cast, opponents and game situation. Segments right of the line add value; left of it take value away. The dot is the total. The quarterback segment is his career effect plus how far that season's plays beat the model.

Quarterback value, adjusted

Estimated EPA per play above an average quarterback with the same play-caller, receivers, opponents and situations. The top 20 of all quarterbacks with 2,000+ plays since 2006, plus these five. Lines are 80% intervals from resampling games.

Play-caller value, adjusted

The same model's estimate for each play-caller, with the quarterback held constant. The top 20 with 3,000+ plays, plus every play-caller these five have had. "(HC)" marks a head coach standing in where no play-caller is listed.

Each play-caller: with him vs with other quarterbacks

Opponent-adjusted EPA per play (each play's EPA minus how much that defense allowed above league average that season). "Others" is the same play-caller's offenses with any other quarterback, 2006 on. Lift is the difference. Model effect is the play-caller's own estimated value, with its league rank.

Game situation: with him vs the play-caller's other quarterbacks

Neutral pass rate over expected (first and second down, win probability 20–80%, first three quarters), average expected points at the snap, share of plays while trailing, average yards to go on third down, and schedule (EPA the opposing defenses allowed above league average; negative means tougher defenses).

Games lost from winning positions

Losses in which his team's win probability reached 75% or more in the second half. The verdict weighs only his own interceptions, lost fumbles and sacks after that peak: QB-driven at 20 WP points or more combined, or any turnover in overtime; shared at 5 to 20; otherwise not on him.

Wins from losing positions

Wins in which his team's win probability fell to 25% or less in the second half, with the WP he added on his own plays from that low point on.

How this was measured

Plays counted
Every dropback (passes, sacks, scrambles) and designed run where he is the play's quarterback. Kneels, spikes and two-point tries are left out. Only games where he had at least 10 dropbacks count.
EPA and CPOE
nflverse's expected points added, credited to the quarterback (qb_epa), and completion percentage over expected on pass attempts.
Win probability added
The change in his team's chance of winning on each play, from the nflverse model. Overtime is excluded: the model is unreliable there. It put San Francisco at 99% before a field goal in the Super Bowl LVIII overtime, and it credited Allen's game-losing overtime interception at Denver with a gain.
Miscues
An interception he threw, a fumble he lost, or a sack he took. A costly miscue cost his team 10 WP points or more on one play.
Late and close
Fourth quarter and overtime with the score within 8 points. Trailing late means down by 1 to 8 in the same window.
Reads
FTN charting via nflverse, 2022 on. Passer rating uses the NFL formula on the throws in each bucket. Turnover-worthy rate is FTN's interception-worthy flag per attempt. Read ranks are among quarterbacks who meet the dropback minimum and threw at least 20 passes of that kind in the season (8 in 2026, 60 for 2022–26, where the dropback minimum is 1,000).
December splits
Games dated December 1 or later, playoffs included, using nflverse roof and kickoff weather. Dome and closed-roof games are indoor; open-air and open-roof games are outdoor. Passer rating is the NFL formula without spikes, so it can differ from the official figure by about a point.
Supporting cast
Targets are pass attempts with a listed receiver (no sacks, spikes or two-point tries), 2006 to 2026. Each receiver's rates with other passers are pulled toward his position's league average by 50 targets' worth before building the cast baseline. Proven-receiver lift uses only receivers with 100+ targets from other passers, unadjusted. Baselines span different teams, schemes and ages, so treat them as context, not a controlled test.
Coaching model
Ridge regression of play EPA on quarterback, play-caller, defense-season, receiver quality and situation (down and distance, field position, score, quarter, home, season), 716,000 plays from 2006 on. The penalty is chosen by cross-validation over games; intervals come from 30 resamples of games. A quarterback on a running play is the one who last dropped back for that team in the game.
Ranks
Among quarterbacks with 250 or more dropbacks in that season (75 for 2026 so far), all games included.
